Indwelling Sin
in-DWEL-ing sin
n.
“Indwelling” from in- + “dwell” (Old English dwellan, to remain). The phrase comes from Paul’s “sin that dwelleth in me” (Romans 7), the remaining corruption in the believer.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Indwelling sin is the remaining corruption that abides in believers even after their regeneration—the relics of the old nature against which the Christian must wage lifelong war, distinguished from the reigning sin that still rules the unregenerate. Though the dominion of sin is broken at conversion, so that sin no longer reigns as lord over the believer, its presence is not yet abolished; a fountain of indwelling corruption remains, lusting against the Spirit, ever active to tempt, hinder, and defile. Paul, writing as a regenerate man, gives the classic description: that which I do I allow not; for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I... it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me. He finds a law in his members warring against the law of his mind, and cries out, O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? This indwelling sin is not the believer’s true and dominant self—he delights in the law of God after the inward man—but a defeated yet still-present enemy within the camp. The doctrine, expounded with unmatched power by the Puritan John Owen, accounts for the believer’s ongoing struggle, guards against both presumption and despair, and grounds the lifelong duty of mortification: the Christian is to be killing sin, by the Spirit, all his days, knowing that indwelling sin will not be wholly eradicated until glory, but that it can and must be daily weakened, resisted, and put to death. To understand indwelling sin is to understand why the holiest saints groan most over their corruption, and why the warfare of the Christian life does not end this side of heaven.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines INDWELLING as residence within, or in the heart; the “indwelling sin” is the remaining corruption that dwells in the regenerate.

expand to see more

INDWELLING, n. — Residence within, or in the heart or soul.

INDWELLING, a. — Dwelling within; remaining in the heart; as indwelling sin, the corruption that remains in the believer, or indwelling grace, the gracious presence of the Spirit.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 7:17 — "Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me."

Romans 7:23-24 — "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind... O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"

Galatians 5:17 — "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other."

Romans 8:13 — "...but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

No major postmodern redefinition, but the doctrine is lost from two sides—perfectionism that denies any remaining sin in the believer, and an antinomian ease that excuses indwelling sin instead of warring against it.

expand to see more

The doctrine of indwelling sin is lost to two opposite errors. The first is perfectionism, which teaches that the truly consecrated believer may attain, in this life, a state free from sin—whether by a second blessing, an entire sanctification, or a higher-life surrender that eradicates the corrupt nature. This flatly contradicts Paul, who, as a mature apostle, confessed the sin that dwelt in him and the law in his members warring against his mind. Perfectionism breeds either pride in those who imagine they have arrived, or crushing despair in the honest soul who knows he has not; and it always requires redefining sin downward until the remaining corruption no longer counts.

The opposite error is the antinomian ease that, granting indwelling sin remains, uses its permanence as an excuse rather than a summons—“I am only human, sin will always be with me, so why strive?” This turns a doctrine meant to fuel warfare into a pillow for sloth. But Scripture never permits the believer to make peace with his indwelling enemy; it commands him to mortify the deeds of the body by the Spirit, to be killing sin lest sin be killing him, as Owen famously pressed. The right doctrine holds the tension: sin remains in the believer and will not be wholly eradicated until glory, so perfectionism is false; yet sin is no longer to reign, and must be daily resisted and put to death, so antinomian ease is false. The Christian life is therefore neither sinless triumph nor comfortable defeat, but lifelong, Spirit-empowered war against an enemy already dethroned but not yet destroyed.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on Paul’s sin that dwelleth (oikeō, to indwell) in him, the flesh (sarx) warring against the Spirit, to be put to death (thanatoō).

Usage

"Indwelling sin is the remaining corruption in the believer—dethroned at conversion, but not yet destroyed."

"Owen pressed the duty of mortification: be killing sin, or it will be killing you."

"Perfectionism denies indwelling sin; antinomian ease excuses it; the gospel commands war against it."
